## Situation

At 13:10 UTC I was paged because the synthetic monitor "checkout-journey" has failed 3 times in a row since 13:02 UTC. All failures come from a single probe location (sa-east).

Evidence pointing to a localized, likely non-severe issue:
- Real-user error rate across all locations is 0.3% against a 0.2% baseline, a small deviation.
- Orders per minute are 9, normal for this hour, so checkout is completing for real users overall.
- The CDN provider announced maintenance on its sa-east edge starting at 13:00 UTC, two minutes before the first failure.
- There have been no deployments today, so an internal code change is unlikely to be the cause.

Evidence pointing to real user impact in Brazil:
- 2 support tickets say "the page won't load", both from Brazil.

Working hypothesis: the CDN sa-east maintenance is degrading access for some users in the sa-east region. This is a hypothesis, not a confirmed cause.

Information I do not have:
- The size of the sa-east user base and the real-user error rate for sa-east alone (the 0.3% figure is global and could hide a regional spike).
- The exact failure mode seen by the probe (timeout, 5xx, DNS, TLS).
- The scope and expected duration of the CDN maintenance, and whether the provider expects customer impact.
- Whether other probe locations exist and are passing (I only know the failures came from one location).
- Whether there is a fallback or alternate CDN route.

Assumptions: the probe is functioning correctly; the 2 tickets are related to the same event; no other changes (config, third-party, infrastructure) occurred outside deployments.

## Actions

1. Acknowledge the page and declare a low-severity incident (suspected regional degradation) so work is tracked, while keeping the option to escalate.
2. Segment real-user metrics (error rate, latency, orders) for Brazil/sa-east only, to test whether the global 0.3% hides a regional problem.
3. Inspect the failing probe runs to identify the failure mode (timeout, HTTP status, DNS, TLS) and at which step of the checkout journey it fails.
4. Check the CDN provider's status page and maintenance notice for scope, duration and any known impact; open a ticket or contact the provider if the details are unclear.
5. Check whether the same journey passes from other probe locations or from a manual test through a sa-east path, to confirm the issue is regional.
6. Do not roll back or change anything in the application: there were no deployments, and a change would add risk without addressing the suspected cause.
7. If the sa-east segment shows a clear impact and a fallback or alternate CDN route exists, evaluate shifting sa-east traffic to it. Only do this if the segmented data supports it.

## Decision rationale

- The monitor failure is real but narrow: one location, with the timing matching the announced CDN maintenance window. That makes the CDN the most plausible cause.
- Global user health looks essentially normal (0.3% vs 0.2% baseline, normal order volume), so this does not justify a high-severity response, a rollback or waking additional teams.
- The 2 Brazilian tickets show some users are affected, so I cannot treat it as a pure monitor false positive. I will not dismiss it.
- With no deployments, rolling back would not help and would add risk.
- The cheapest, highest-value next step is segmenting sa-east data, since it can confirm or rule out meaningful regional impact. I would escalate if that data shows elevated errors or dropping orders in Brazil, if the probe failures continue after the maintenance window ends, or if the failures spread to other locations. I would downgrade or close if sa-east metrics are normal and the probe recovers when maintenance ends.
- Confidence is moderate, not high: the causal link to the CDN is inferred from timing alone.

## Communications

CDN sa-east maintenance started 13:00 UTC; suspected cause, unconfirmed. 2 Brazil support tickets. No deploys today. Investigating sa-east-specific impact; next update in 30 minutes or on change."
- Support: tell the team the likely cause is a CDN maintenance window affecting some Brazil users. Ask them to tag any further "page won't load" tickets from Brazil and report the count and timestamps. Do not promise a resolution time, because I do not know the maintenance duration.
- Customers: no public status update yet. If the sa-east segmentation confirms meaningful impact, I will publish a short regional notice for Brazil users.
- CDN provider: request confirmation of maintenance scope, expected duration and any known customer impact on sa-east.
- Updates will go out every 30 minutes (assumed cadence) or sooner if the situation changes.

## Next steps

- By about 13:30 UTC: complete the sa-east segmentation and probe failure analysis, then decide whether to keep, raise or lower the severity.
- Confirm the maintenance window end time with the CDN provider and check whether the probe recovers afterward. If it recovers, treat the CDN as the cause and close the incident.
- If the probe keeps failing after maintenance ends, or other locations start failing, escalate and widen the investigation beyond the CDN.
- Keep monitoring Brazil support tickets, the global error rate and orders per minute.
- After resolution: record the timeline; review whether the alert should factor in announced provider maintenance windows or require more than one probe location before paging; and ask whether a regional fallback for the CDN exists or is needed.

## Situation

**Declared at 16:27 UTC: SEV-1 (highest tier of the scale), commander: me (the paged responder).**

Known facts:
- Since 16:20 UTC all card payments fail with "authorization timeout". Bank transfer works.
- Card payments are about 85% of revenue, so paying customers are affected and most revenue is blocked.
- No deployments or configuration changes in the last 3 days. A local change is therefore an unlikely cause.
- The payment provider's status page says "investigating elevated latency". Their API now answers in about 25 s at the median.
- Our client timeout is 30 s with 3 automatic retries, so one checkout can hold a worker for up to 90 s.
- Worker threads are saturated. Browsing pages are also degraded (p99 6 s, normally 400 ms). The incident is spreading from checkout to the whole storefront.

Severity justification: paying customers are affected, the majority of revenue is blocked, and impact is widening (browsing now degraded). Each of these independently triggers escalation. No root cause or ETA from the provider exists yet.

Current understanding (hypothesis, not confirmed): the provider's latency is the trigger. Our timeout and retry settings turn that into worker exhaustion, which is why unrelated pages are slow. The provider's slowness is outside our control. The worker exhaustion is within our control and is what we mitigate first.

Unknowns and assumptions (stated explicitly):
- The briefing does not give the severity scale, so I assume SEV-1 is the top tier.
- It does not say whether card authorization and browsing share one worker pool. The symptoms strongly suggest they do. I assume they do.
- It does not say whether a feature flag, circuit breaker, or per-route concurrency limit already exists. I assume at least one fast control (a flag or config toggle for the card payment option, or a timeout/retry setting) can be changed without a deploy. If not, a rapid deploy is the fallback.
- It does not say whether payment requests carry idempotency keys, nor whether a timed-out authorization may still have succeeded at the provider. I assume this is unknown and treat it as a possible data-integrity risk (duplicate authorizations or holds from retries, orders whose payment state is uncertain). Under the escalation rules this is already covered by SEV-1, and it must be checked.
- I have no information on whether other providers or a fallback card acquirer are integrated. I assume none.
- Provider ETA: none given.

## Actions

Roles (declared 16:27–16:30): Commander (me, owns decisions and timeline); Technical lead (on-call backend engineer, drives diagnosis and executes mitigations); Communications lead (owns customer, support and executive updates); Scribe (keeps one shared timestamped log of every action and finding). If staffing is thin, I hold commander only and pull in a second engineer rather than combine commander and technical lead.

Mitigation first, root cause later. In priority order, each timeboxed to 15 minutes before pivoting:

1. **Protect the storefront (target within 15 minutes of declaration, by about 16:42).** Stop card checkouts from consuming the shared worker capacity. Preferred order of options:
   a. Cut the card-authorization timeout and retries via config or flag: lower the timeout well below 30 s and reduce retries from 3 to 0 or 1 for card authorization. This reduces worst-case hold time from 90 s to a small fraction. Note that with a 25 s median, a short timeout will fail many card payments that might have succeeded. Those payments are already failing for customers, so we accept the trade-off.
   b. Put card authorization behind its own bounded concurrency limit (bulkhead), or open a circuit breaker for the provider, so excess card attempts fail fast and browsing workers stay free.
   c. If neither is available quickly, turn the card payment option off at checkout (flag) and show a clear message directing customers to bank transfer. This is the safest fallback because card payments are failing anyway, and it restores browsing at once.
2. **Verify with metrics, not appearance.** Success looks like: worker utilization drops from saturation, browsing p99 returns toward 400 ms normal, checkout error responses return fast, and queue depth drains. Record the numbers with timestamps.
3. **Make bank transfer the visible alternative** at checkout and in the failure message, so revenue is not lost entirely.
4. **Data-integrity check (parallel, assigned to a second engineer).** Determine whether timed-out card attempts may have created authorizations, charges or holds at the provider, and whether any orders are in an ambiguous payment state. Check idempotency handling on retries. Do not auto-retry or auto-cancel affected orders until this is understood. List the affected orders for later reconciliation.
5. **Open a channel to the provider** (support or account contact) in addition to watching the status page: ask for scope, cause and ETA, and whether authorizations that timed out were processed.
6. **Keep monitoring** for 15 to 30 minutes after mitigation before any "resolved" decision. Re-enable card payments only after provider latency is back within normal range, confirmed by our own metrics, and then re-enable gradually (watch worker utilization while ramping).

Timeline log (scribe): 16:20 card failures begin (from alert); 16:27 paged, SEV-1 declared; further entries added with timestamps as actions happen.

## Decision rationale

- **Severity before troubleshooting.** The majority of revenue (about 85%) is blocked, customers are paying customers, and impact is widening to browsing. Any one of those justifies the top tier. Declaring high costs little; declaring low would under-resource and under-communicate.
- **Mitigate our own amplification, not the provider.** We cannot fix the provider's latency. The one thing under our control is how long a failing dependency can hold our workers. With a 25 s median against a 30 s timeout and 3 retries, each checkout can pin a worker for up to 90 s, and the saturation that slows browsing follows from that. Cutting hold time or isolating card traffic addresses the spreading damage directly.
- **Accepting more card failures is the right trade.** Card payments are already failing, so tightening timeouts or disabling the card option costs little additional revenue, while protecting the other traffic and bank-transfer checkout. Shortening timeouts may cause a few more failures for slow-but-successful authorizations, which is why the data-integrity check runs in parallel.
- **Why not wait for the provider.** Their status page says only "investigating", with no ETA. Waiting leaves the storefront degraded for an unknown time. Recovery on their side does not fix our retry and timeout design either, so waiting would also leave us exposed to a repeat.
- **Why not look for a local cause first.** No changes in 3 days and the provider's own acknowledgement make a local cause unlikely. We keep a timeboxed check (15 minutes) of our own network path and error logs in parallel, but mitigation does not wait for it.
- **Option chosen order.** Config or flag changes (1a, 1b) are fastest and most reversible and keep card payments partially working if the provider recovers quickly. Disabling the card option (1c) is the guaranteed backstop. If mitigation 1 does not show improvement in metrics within 15 minutes, pivot to the next option.
- **Why no auto-retry of ambiguous payments.** Retrying or cancelling without knowing whether the provider processed the first attempt could double-charge or orphan funds. This is a data-integrity concern and it is investigated before any bulk action.
- **Blameless framing.** The system allowed a single slow dependency to exhaust shared capacity. No person caused this, and the review will focus on timeout, retry and isolation design.

## Communications

Cadence for SEV-1: update every 30 minutes (assumed; adjust to the organization's standard if it differs), even when nothing has changed, plus an immediate notice on any major change. Each update states status, impact, current understanding, actions taken and the time of the next update.

**Initial notice (internal, send by about 16:35 UTC):**
"SEV-1 declared 16:27 UTC. Since 16:20 UTC all card payments on the storefront fail with authorization timeouts; bank transfer works. Card payments are about 85% of revenue. Browsing pages are also slow because worker threads are saturated. Current understanding: the payment provider is reporting elevated latency (their API answers in about 25 s at the median) and our timeout and retry settings are holding workers for up to 90 s per checkout. No deployments or config changes in 3 days. Actions: roles assigned; reducing card-authorization hold time / isolating card traffic to protect the rest of the storefront; contacting the provider; checking for any ambiguous payment states. Next update at [time + 30 min]."

**Customer-facing / support message (when mitigation is applied or the card option is disabled):**
"We are experiencing problems processing card payments. You can still pay by bank transfer. We are working with our payment provider and will update you as soon as card payments are restored. If a card payment failed or showed an error, please check before retrying, so you are not charged twice." Support receives a short brief with the same facts and the rule: do not promise refunds or timelines yet; escalate any report of a double charge to the incident channel.

**Periodic updates:** same five fields every 30 minutes, including "no change" when true, with the latest metrics (browsing p99, worker utilization, card failure rate).

**Provider contact:** the communications lead or technical lead records every provider response with a timestamp in the shared log.

**Resolution notice:** sent only after metrics are back within normal range and have held for 15 to 30 minutes after mitigation or after card payments are re-enabled. It states duration, impact, what was done, any customers needing follow-up (ambiguous payments) and that a review follows.

## Next steps

Immediate (next 30 minutes):
- Commander: confirm roles and severity in the incident channel; set the update cadence and timestamps.
- Technical lead: apply mitigation 1a/1b/1c in that order, timeboxed to 15 minutes each, and report the metric changes to the scribe.
- Second engineer: start the data-integrity check (ambiguous payments, idempotency, duplicate holds) and list affected orders.
- Communications lead: send the initial notice and prepare the customer and support messages.
- Commander: obtain the provider's scope, cause and ETA through a direct contact.

Recovery and closure:
- Confirm browsing p99 and worker utilization are back to normal. Then monitor 15 to 30 minutes.
- Re-enable card payments gradually only once the provider's latency is confirmed normal by our own measurements. Keep the tightened timeout and retry settings in place until the review decides the permanent values.
- Send the resolution notice and all-clear.

Blameless post-incident review within 48 hours, with impact, timeline, contributing factors, what went well, what went poorly, and action items each with an owner, a priority and a deadline (owners and dates to be assigned in the review; none are assumed here). Candidate action items:
- Review client timeout and retry policy for card authorization (30 s with 3 retries allows 90 s worker hold).
- Isolate card payment calls from browsing capacity (separate worker pool or concurrency limit).
- Add a circuit breaker and fast-fail behavior for the payment provider.
- Add alerting on provider latency and on worker saturation so this is detected before payment failures.
- Ensure idempotency on authorization retries and a reconciliation process for ambiguous payments.
- Evaluate a secondary payment path or provider (open question: none known to exist).
- Prepare a pre-written feature flag and runbook to disable card payments with a bank-transfer message.

## Situation

- Since 08:12 UTC, 62% of requests to the platform fail in eu-west. us-east and ap-south are healthy. I was paged at 08:19 UTC, so the impact is at least 7 minutes old.
- The likely trigger is a rate-limit configuration push to eu-west only at 08:10 UTC. The failures began 2 minutes later. This is a hypothesis built on timing, not a confirmed cause.
- Scope: eu-west carries 22% of global traffic. If failures are spread evenly, about 13.6% of global requests are failing (0.62 x 0.22). That is an estimate. The briefing does not say whether the 62% covers all eu-west traffic.
- Severity: declared SEV1 (highest tier). Justification: a majority of requests in a whole region are failing, and the failure has already run 7 minutes. Two further points support it. The briefing does not say whether paying customers are affected. I assume they are, because this is a platform-wide failure, and that assumption alone triggers escalation. The same push is scheduled for the other regions tomorrow, so the problem could spread. If the team's severity scale is defined differently, re-map this classification. Escalation is immediate: page the on-call leads and notify leadership.
- Roles. The briefing names nobody, so these are assignments to confirm now:
  - Incident commander: me.
  - Technical lead: the eu-west on-call engineer.
  - Communications lead: to be named by the commander.
  - Scribe: to be named by the commander.
  - All four must acknowledge before troubleshooting starts.
- Unknown, and to be collected by the technical lead:
  - Whether any data-integrity concern exists. None is stated. If one appears, severity rises automatically.
  - Whether the failing requests are rejected by the new rate-limit settings. This matches the push but is unconfirmed.
  - Whether paying and EU customers are specifically affected.

## Actions

Timeline (UTC). Times up to 08:19 come from the briefing. Later times are targets, and the scribe records the real times.

- 08:10: configuration push (rate-limit settings) to eu-west only. Source: briefing.
- 08:12: 62% of eu-west requests start failing. Source: briefing.
- 08:19: page received. I declare SEV1, state the impact (62% failures in eu-west, about 13.6% of global traffic by estimate) and name myself commander. The other roles are assigned and a single shared incident record with timestamps is opened.
- 08:20 (target): freeze all configuration pushes. The same push scheduled for the other regions tomorrow is on hold. No further changes go to any region until the incident is closed.
- 08:21 (target): the commander orders mitigation and the technical lead starts restoring the previous configuration version in eu-west. This takes about 4 minutes, so it should finish around 08:25.
- Parallel diagnosis, timeboxed to 15 minutes: the technical lead compares the new and old rate-limit settings against the failing responses. This is not a blocker for the rollback. If the rate-limit hypothesis is not confirmed or ruled out in 15 minutes, pivot to the next hypothesis. Candidates are other changes in the same window or a regional dependency.
- Verify the rollback by metrics, not by appearance. Check that the eu-west error rate returns to its baseline and objective, that the failures stop, and that no error pattern has appeared in us-east or ap-south.
- After recovery, keep monitoring for 15 to 30 minutes. If the metrics hold, declare the incident resolved and send the all-clear.
- Fallback if the rollback fails or does not reduce errors: escalate to the next level and re-evaluate. Do not shift EU traffic out of the region (see the rationale below).

## Decision rationale

- Mitigate first, root cause second. A tested restore path exists: the previous configuration version can be restored in eu-west in about 4 minutes, and it targets the change that coincides with the onset of failures. Waiting for a full root cause would extend the impact.
- Roll back instead of shifting traffic by DNS weights. Two reasons:
  - The policy says personal data of EU customers must be processed only in the EU region. Moving eu-west traffic to us-east or ap-south would risk sending EU personal data outside the EU. I have no information that lets me separate EU personal-data traffic from the rest. A policy violation would be a second incident on top of the first.
  - The DNS TTL is 5 minutes, so the shift would likely be slower than, or comparable to, the 4 minute rollback. It would also move load onto healthy regions that are not known to have spare capacity.
- A partial DNS shift of only non-personal-data traffic is not proposed. I do not know whether the traffic can be split that way, and it adds risk.
- Freezing the other regions is cheap and removes the chance of the failure spreading tomorrow. The push should not go out until the cause is understood.
- Blameless framing: the system allowed a configuration change to reach a whole region without a canary or automatic rollback, as far as the briefing shows. The review will look at that gap and not at who pushed the change. It is unknown whether such safeguards exist, and the review should check.
- Assumptions to correct if wrong: the rollback restores the same service state as before 08:10; the 62% failures stem from the push; failure is evenly spread across eu-west traffic.

## Communications

Cadence: SEV1 updates every 15 minutes, even if the update is that nothing has changed and the investigation continues. This cadence is an assumption. Use the organization's own cadence if it differs. Each update states status, impact, current understanding, actions taken and the time of the next update.

Initial notice (send by 08:25, owner: communications lead):
> Status: investigating, SEV1. Impact: since 08:12 UTC about 62% of requests in eu-west are failing. Other regions are healthy. Current understanding: the failures began shortly after a rate-limit configuration change in eu-west at 08:10 UTC. This is not yet confirmed as the cause. Actions: we are restoring the previous configuration in eu-west (about 4 minutes) and have frozen further configuration changes. We are not moving EU traffic out of the EU region. Next update: 15 minutes from this notice.

Periodic update (every 15 minutes): the same five fields, with real error-rate figures once measured.

Resolution notice (after 15 to 30 minutes of stable metrics, owner: communications lead):
> Status: resolved. Impact: eu-west requests failed at about 62% from 08:12 UTC until [time of recovery, from the incident record]. Cause: [confirmed cause, or "under review" if not yet confirmed]. Actions: the previous configuration was restored and metrics are back within objectives. A blameless review will follow within 48 hours.

Audiences: internal engineering and leadership at once; customer-facing updates for eu-west customers per the usual status channel. Whether the organization has contractual notice duties to paying or EU customers is unknown and should be checked with the owner of customer communications.

## Next steps

1. Within 48 hours: hold the blameless post-incident review. It covers impact, timeline, contributing factors, what went well, what went poorly, and action items. Owner: commander to schedule; scribe supplies the timeline.
2. Do not run the scheduled push to the other regions until the cause is confirmed and the fix has been validated in a safe way. Owner: technical lead. Deadline: before tomorrow's scheduled push.
3. Confirm the root cause, for example which rate-limit setting produced the failures. Owner: technical lead. Deadline: before the review.
4. Review how a regional configuration push can be staged (canary to a small share of traffic first, automatic rollback on error-rate rise). Owners and dates to be assigned in the review; I do not know what already exists.
5. Check whether any data-integrity or data-residency issue occurred. Nothing in the briefing suggests it, but this should be confirmed from logs. Owner: technical lead.
6. Every action item gets a named owner, a priority and a deadline, and is tracked to completion.
